meta.description: Why can't a single cell grow as big as a football? How long is a stretch of DNA, and why must it be packed so tightly? This short illustrated sample answers both with one line of geometry, a rotatable 3D model of the double helix drawn to scale, and worked examples whose every number is checked by code.

preface.text: This is a one-chapter gallery sample for the biology profile. It shows how a Scriptorium book handles a **3D structure built from cited dimensions**: on the web you can rotate the DNA double helix; in print and in the ebook you get three fixed views, and in print a QR code that opens the interactive model.

preface.title: Safety
preface.text: This book explains biology; it is not a laboratory protocol. Work with living organisms, tissues or DNA only under the biosafety rules of a supervised laboratory.

chapters.title: Small Cells, Long Molecules
goals: Explain why the ratio of surface area to volume limits how large a cell can grow.
Calculate that ratio for a spherical cell of any radius.
Describe the shape of the DNA double helix and calculate the length and number of turns of a stretch of DNA.

summary.text: Everything a cell takes in or gets rid of has to cross its outer membrane. As a cell grows, its volume grows faster than its surface, so each cubic micrometre (µm³) of cell is served by less membrane. Past a certain size, the membrane can no longer keep up — one reason most cells are microscopic [@openstax-bio2e, §4.2].

intuition.text: Think of a cell as a factory whose only doors are in its outside walls. Double the length of every wall and the floor space inside grows eightfold, but the wall area — and so the number of doors — grows only fourfold. The bigger the factory, the longer the queue at each door.

formal.text: The textbook models a cell as a sphere, with surface area $4\pi r^2$ and volume $4\pi r^3/3$ [@openstax-bio2e, §4.2]. Dividing one by the other gives the [[surface area to volume ratio]].

formal.intuition: Surface grows with the square of the radius and volume with the cube, so their ratio shrinks in proportion to the radius.

where.meaning: radius of the cell (half its diameter)

example.text: A cell of radius 1 µm (diameter 2 µm, within the 0.1–5.0 µm the textbook gives for prokaryotes) has $A/V = 3/1 = 3$ per µm. A cell of radius 10 µm (diameter 20 µm, within the 10–100 µm range for eukaryotes) has $A/V = 3/10 = 0.3$ per µm [@openstax-bio2e, §4.2]. Ten times the radius leaves one tenth of the membrane per unit of volume.

formal.validity: Exact for a sphere only. Real cells are rarely spheres; long, thin or folded shapes keep more surface per volume, which is one way large cells cope. The ratio has units of 1/length, so its value depends on the unit you measure $r$ in.

formal.alt: Plot of surface area divided by volume, in units per micrometre, against cell radius from 0.5 to 20 micrometres on a logarithmic axis; a falling curve passes 3 per micrometre at a radius of 1 micrometre and 0.3 per micrometre at 10 micrometres.
formal.caption: For a spherical cell the ratio $A/V = 3/r$ falls as the cell grows: a cell ten times wider has one tenth of the membrane per unit of volume.

limits.title: Simplification
limits.text: Diffusion across the membrane is only one limit on cell size. The sphere model shows the direction of the effect, not the exact largest size any particular cell can reach.

takeaways: Surface area grows as $r^2$, volume as $r^3$.
For a sphere, $A/V = 3/r$: ten times the radius, one tenth the ratio.
Less membrane per volume means slower supply, which keeps most cells small.

summary.text: DNA is two strands wound around each other in a double helix. Each strand has a sugar–phosphate backbone on the outside; the bases point inward, and a base on one strand pairs with a base on the other — adenine (A) with thymine (T), guanine (G) with cytosine (C) [@openstax-bio2e, §14.2]. Each pair is a [[base pair]].

intuition.text: Picture a ladder twisted like a spiral staircase. The two rails are the backbones, each rung is a base pair, and every rung is turned a little relative to the one below, so after ten rungs the staircase has made one full turn.

formal.text: The textbook gives three dimensions: the helix is 2 nm across, neighbouring base pairs are 0.34 nm apart, and one turn is 3.4 nm long, so there are 10 base pairs per turn [@openstax-bio2e, §14.2]. Each base pair is therefore rotated $360\degree / 10 = 36\degree$ from the one before. The model below is built from exactly these numbers.

formal.alt: Ball-and-stick model of one turn of a DNA double helix: orange beads for the two sugar–phosphate backbones spiral around the outside, blue beads for the paired bases meet in the middle; looking down the axis the backbones form a ring 2 nanometres across.
formal.caption: One turn of the DNA double helix, 10 base pairs, drawn to scale from the textbook's dimensions: 2 nm diameter, 0.34 nm between base pairs, 3.4 nm per turn [@openstax-bio2e, §14.2]. Outer (orange) beads mark the backbones; inner (blue) beads stand for the bases. Simplified: each base is a single bead and the two backbones sit exactly opposite each other, so the major and minor grooves of real DNA are not shown.
formal.credit: Schematic model built by examples/cells-and-dna/figures.ts from the cited dimensions.

formal.intuition: Each base pair adds the same small step along the axis, so length is just the number of steps times the step size.

where.meaning: length of the DNA along the helix axis

example.text: A stretch of 1,500 base pairs is $1500 \times 0.34 = 510$ nm long — about half a micrometre, already a quarter of the diameter of the 2 µm cell in the previous section.

formal.validity: Uses the textbook's average rise of 0.34 nm per base pair for the common double-helix form [@openstax-bio2e, §14.2]. Inside cells DNA is wound around proteins and folded, so the space it occupies is far smaller than this stretched-out length.

formal.intuition: Ten base pairs make one full turn, so counting turns is counting base pairs in tens.

example.text: The same 1,500 base pairs make $1500 / 10 = 150$ turns, and $150 \times 3.4$ nm $= 510$ nm, matching Eq. (eq-dna-length).

formal.validity: Ten base pairs per turn is the textbook's average for the double helix [@openstax-bio2e, §14.2]; the exact figure varies slightly with sequence and conditions.

limits.title: What the model leaves out
limits.text: Real DNA has a wide major groove and a narrow minor groove where proteins bind [@openstax-bio2e, §14.2]. This model places the two backbones exactly opposite each other, which hides the grooves; its diameter, rise and turn length are to scale, its beads are not.

takeaways: DNA is a double helix 2 nm across with 10 base pairs per 3.4 nm turn.
A pairs with T and G pairs with C.
Length along the axis is $0.34$ nm per base pair; turns are base pairs divided by ten.

summary: A sphere's surface-to-volume ratio is $3/r$, so bigger cells have less membrane per unit of volume.
DNA is a double helix 2 nm wide; each base pair adds 0.34 nm and turns the helix by $36\degree$.
Simple geometry explains both why cells are small and why DNA must be packed tightly.

glossary.definition: Two bases, one on each strand of DNA, joined in the middle of the double helix: adenine with thymine, or guanine with cytosine.
A cell's outer surface area divided by its volume; for a sphere it equals 3 divided by the radius.
